data.translation: He says, ‘Really, nobody has returned from this way, (but) you’ve returned!’

rationale: First I ko-Preterit example; ko- with qaṭəl daʕir-at, contrasted with unprefixed daʕǝr.

summary: New box ko-Preterit: example for sense 1 in ko-Preterit (57/125)

data.translation: Er dachte: "Gott sei gedankt! Nachdem meine Brüder umgekehrt sind und nicht getötet wurden, und auch ich zurückgekommen bin, werden wir einander wiedersehen."

rationale: Second ko-Preterit example; k- plus daʕənno complements the 2sg kodaʕirat evidence.

summary: New box Infectum: example for sense 1 in Infectum (Jan 2.8/1910)

data.translation: Jan: Father, afterwards, in the new generation, has there been no activity and effort to return music to the church?

rationale: First III Detransitive Infectum example; the full question supplies theme and goal. English is the supplied project machine translation, not an edition translation; analysis rests on the Turoyo.

data.translation: <...> He too had come from military service, he had come, he was a soldier of France; he had returned and had come, he would say, ‘I perform magic.’ <...>

summary: New idiom: daʕər/doʕər ʕal ruḥo 'wieder zu sich kommen, wieder zu Kräften kommen'

data.headword: daʕər/doʕər ʕal ruḥo 'wieder zu sich kommen, wieder zu Kräften kommen'
data.turoyo: Hul arbʕi yawme d saymutəlli more, bu baṣro daf fare w d obutəlli u štoyayḏi ḥamro, gdoʕanno ʕal ruḥi w ktoweno xd meqəm qawyo.
data.translation: Wenn ihr mich vierzig Tage lang pflegt, mit Lammfleisch, und mir Wein zu trinken gebt, werde ich wieder zu mir selbst kommen und so stark werden wie früher.

rationale: Distinct reflexive recovery collocation, one attestation; lookup search ʕal ruḥ found no existing dʕr recovery idiom. Meaning belongs to I.2. Independently corroborated in batch 2 at 97/44.

summary: New idiom: daʕər/doʕər lebo laf- 'sich jemandem in Zuneigung zuwenden'

data.headword: daʕər/doʕər lebo laf- 'sich jemandem in Zuneigung zuwenden'
data.turoyo: Hama d doʕər lebe laf eli, be ma lə gmaḥarwalliyo?
data.translation: Wenn sich nur erst sein Herz mir zuwendet, ob ich ihn mir dann nicht verführen kann?

rationale: One clear affectional heart-turning collocation; already quoted under ḥrw III.2, confirmed by lookup, but not listed as a dʕr idiom.

summary: New idiom: madʕalle/madʕər foṯo laf- 'jemandem sein Antlitz zuwenden, Gunst erweisen'

data.headword: madʕalle/madʕər foṯo laf- 'jemandem sein Antlitz zuwenden, Gunst erweisen'

data.translation: und gerade heute hat Gott uns sein Antlitz zugewandt, unsere Frauen sind beide schwanger.

rationale: Divine favour is established by the face-turning construction and the following pregnancies; lookup found no existing matching dʕr idiom. Source poṯe is preserved in the example.

summary: New idiom: madʕalle/madʕər ʕawḏ̣iye 'eine Wohltat vergelten'

rationale: Repayment collocation under III.1 vergelten. Lookup ʕawḏ̣ found only cognate ʕwḏ̣/yfy passages, no existing dʕr idiom; do not infer a separate simple-verb sense.

summary: New idiom: daʕər/doʕər lebo mən 'Widerwillen gegen etwas empfinden'

summary: I typically codes the returner as S, with l-, ʕal-, gab or an implicit destination. III adds an agent and patient; restored-state predicates may be bare (ənsan, mšiḥoye). No new Detransitive form is established.

I.3 is inherited as inchoative, but repeated pounding, dressing, bandaging and letter writing predominantly show renewed action. Retain the editors’ label; flag its semantic range without replacing the inherited terminology.

The two I ko-Preterit tokens combine k(o)- with qaṭəl a-vocalism; g-/ko- Infectum also serves narrative and future functions. -wa supports habitual and irrealis contexts, so it is not a past-event test by itself.

The supplied routine counts corroborate common physical return (I Preterit Intransitive 457, Infectum 220) and III answering (Preterit 134). They are not additional quotations and are not independently reanalysed.

Batch 2 preserves batch 1’s technical III.3b and all earlier additions, but adds I.1b after the clear right-turn/other-side evidence. The earlier MAC NE Unfortunate Youth/9 example is reassigned cumulatively to 1b; the original batch-1 files remain intact.

Topic switching recurs across many Ritter narratives; both return-to-topic (l-/laf-/ʕal-/b-) and leave-topic (m-) track motion/withdrawal government. Repetition with a following verb (115/97) remains I.3.

The bodily recovery alternation contrasts a person returning to a former state (I.2), a spirit/strength subject returning to a person (I.1), and the existing ʕal ruḥo recovery idiom. No Detransitive is established.
Recompense at 78/141 and 108/32 is explicitly covered by III.1 vergelten. It does not isolate the wider III.4 restoration/reparation composite sufficiently to renumber or split existing examples.
Several later-reader thin-cell claims use baseline counts, not the cumulative revised entry. Ordinary repeated quotations, rn assimilation and filled cells therefore receive no additional examples.
Jan includes conversational interviews as well as written framing. Speaker alternation and disputed recollections must not be flattened into a single authoritative narrative.

Preterit-wa daʕərwo/daʕəriwo and feminine daʕərowa contrast with Infectum-wa duʕarwo/dəʕrowa. Narrative anteriority is especially clear in 1.21/1087 and 1.28/1326; reductions alone cannot establish a paradigm.
kdaʕər at 1.8/159 has the a-vocalism of ko-Preterit, unlike neighbouring doʕər and dəʕrina. The reader box is corrected; no new sense follows.
III retains r in Madʕarle beside inherited madʕalle. The common answer cells are already sufficiently represented after round 1; a book-title token is no reason to multiply examples.
mitadʕəro at 2.8/1910 is a Detransitive Infectum with theme subject and l-goal. Only the attested form is established, not a complete Detransitive paradigm.
No new collocation survives comparison with round-1 heart-turning and discourse-return material. III.4 restoration/reparation is not newly resolved by this evidence.

Bilgic Die Rolle Məḏyaḏs im Tur Abdin/21: gdoʕər has no overt negative, but the edition says wird nicht zurückkehren. Which witness has the intended polarity? No translation is corrected or quoted as an example.
JTM 1.1/6: does gdoʕər aʕlayye assert spatial returning over the field or only renewed ploughing? It is provisionally filed under I.1.
PrS 83/46: verify Daʕər ba quwe and its subject. Does b- introduce a recovered condition, or is the transcription/segmentation irregular? The proposed construction is withheld.
JTM 3.4/6: is madʕarwulle contracted Infectum-wa or Preterit-wa? The clearer madʕəriwunne supplies the published example.
PrS 37/71: the reader locates the German rendering of daʕər ʕal u bazərgan in verse 72, which is not supplied here. Verify alignment; no example is added from the mismatched verse pair.

III.4 explicitly requests separation of restoring form and recompense. This batch supplies many restoration examples but no new secure recompense contrast; retain the composite sense and existing numbering pending the later batch.

summary: Adversarial ʕal orientation can describe turning back to face an opponent; an inherited example already has a returning attack. Distinguish this from proving a turn in place.
The b-marked content may be a factual statement or a legal complaint, as well as a promise; the shared retraction relation is retained.
Former strength and yearly vineyard youth extend restoration beyond magical bodily transformation.
The turned part may belong to a mare, snake or crop bunch; no new sense follows from the possessor.
Restoration may target religious practice or a family arrangement, while preserving an earlier-state result relation.
A rhetorical inability of butter/a barrel to answer is an inanimate subject extension; a possibly inward response and an initiated appeal do not yet establish separate constructions.
A shield may repel an incoming sword stroke; III.1 abschlagen covers this technical context provisionally.
The recovered patient can be a city/political possession. The Turoyo entails recovery; a specifically military reconquest depends on the narrative.
Narrative-topic return is frequent across Ritter texts, with l-, laf-, ʕal-, and b-; it is broader than a single narrator’s wording.
Inanimate returners include bodily strength, eyes, blood, breath/spirit, troubles and spittle. The spittle image can express irrevocability while retaining a literal return syntax.
Leaving a pursuit or leaving a narrative character has the same m-marked separation frame as abandoning a person or possession.

Religious return (1.8/140; 3.33/909), resuming a topic (2.6/1718 and following), and return of faith or answers support the broad return extensions already recorded in round 1. Do not introduce the proposed religious or discourse senses again. The conversion interpretation at 3.33/909 remains less explicit in the isolated verse.

Turning to a new target extends the round-1 orientation subsense: a government turns against Syriacs and God turns toward people in mercy. Hostility and mercy come from the participants and context, not separate meanings of the verb.
The heart-turning idiom proposed in round 1 is supported in religious loyalty to the fathers, with laf-, ʕal- and aʕlayye. No new sense or duplicate idiom is needed.
Alternating singing and answering in harvest work extends ordinary verbal response into song. The Infectum-wa cell had no answering example after round 1.
A boundary or route can turn back, the navel return to position, or alphabetic progression run back from Taw to Olaf. These are participant/path extensions.
